title: Stale tokens remain valid after tenant API key revocation during org membership update
creator: Asha Patel
description: Summary: Customers reported that API keys they explicitly revoked were still able to perform org-scoped operations for up to several minutes. The issue appears when an org membership or tenant binding change occurs concurrently with key revocation. A stale token or session that was cached in the API gateway or in a Dedicated/Private edge proxy continued to be considered valid for the prior org scope. Affects Hosted API and on-prem/private deployments that use local caching or delayed sync for org metadata.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Create org A and user U with API key K bound to org A
2) Start a long-lived request/stream using K that establishes an in-memory session (e.g., streaming chat or long polling),
3) Trigger an org change: move user U from org A to org B (or revoke K) while the session is active,
4) Observe that requests using K for resources scoped to org A continue to succeed for a short window (30s-5min) depending on cache TTLs
5) Reproducible in Hosted with regional cache and in Dedicated/Private when the local auth cache is not immediately invalidated.
observed_behavior: Revoked API keys or changed org bindings allowed access to resources in the old org for a short period after revocation. Customers reported unauthorized reads and one case of attempting a write that was accepted and later rolled back when the backend rejected it after cache expiration.
expected_behavior: Revocation and org membership changes should be enforced immediately across all frontends and proxies; any cached session should be invalidated or re-validated against central authority before allowing org-scoped access.
root_cause: Race between local/auth-cache TTL-based validation and central control-plane updates. When membership or key state changes occur, not all gateways/proxies proactively pull the update; they rely on TTL expiry. Additionally, the token validation path assumed API key->org mapping was immutable for the lifetime of cached session entries, so revocation signals were ignored until cache expiry.
fix: 1) Short-term: set cache TTL to 5s for auth decision entries for org-bound API keys in Hosted and push an emergency flag for Dedicated/Private packages to reduce local auth cache TTLs. 2) Medium-term: implement subscription-based invalidation: control plane broadcasts revocation events to edge nodes and Dedicated controllers; gateways will immediately invalidate sessions matching key or org membership. 3) Add a check at request start: if request includes a long-lived streaming session, perform an auth revalidation handshake when membership changes are detected for the key's owner.
rollback_plan: If new invalidation causes regressions, revert TTL changes and disable the subscription at edge by feature-flag to restore prior behavior while we iterate. Emergency toggle exists in console to force fallback to central validation at small performance cost.
rollout_plan: Canary deploy the subscription-based invalidation to 10% of Hosted traffic and one Dedicated customer replica. Monitor errors and latency for 24 hours. If stable, ramp to 50% then 100% over 48 hours. Provide on-prem/private install instructions and a package update with migration notes. Coordinate with Support to prepare communication to affected customers.
monitoring: Add metrics: auth_cache_hits, auth_invalidation_events, post_revocation_access_attempts, delayed_denials. Dashboards: per-region post_revocation_access_attempts and median auth latency. Alert if >1 post_revocation_access_attempts per minute in canary or >20 across production.
